cim_eredeti: AI Agent Tool Calling in TypeScript: Runaway Loop Guardrails
szoveg_eredeti:
Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most LLM SDKs provide no built-in circuit breaker for agent-level tool-calling loops. This tutorial walks through building a provider-agnostic TypeScript agent loop protected by four discrete guardrails: per-tool attempt caps, execution timeouts, a best-effort token budget guard, and an application-side fallback to draft state.

In April 2026, a developer on Reddit's r/cursor described an agent that got stuck in a loop and ran up more than $2,000 in charges in under two hours while they were away from the keyboard. The agent was not malicious. It kept doing what it was asked, and nothing in the system told it to stop.

This is the core problem. Most LLM SDKs provide no built-in circuit breaker for agent-level tool-calling loops. (Some newer SDKs, such as OpenAI's Agents SDK, now include configurable turn limits, but this is not yet universal.) The model decides when to stop calling tools, and if the tools keep returning errors or the model keeps hallucinating arguments, the loop continues indefinitely, burning tokens and dollars with every iteration.

This tutorial walks through building a provider-agnostic TypeScript agent loop protected by four discrete guardrails: per-tool attempt caps, execution timeouts, a best-effort token budget guard, and an application-side fallback to draft state. Prerequisites include working knowledge of TypeScript, comfort with async/await, and familiarity with sending chat-completion requests and handling tool-call responses.

The canonical agent loop follows a predictable cycle: send a conversation history to the LLM, receive a response that may contain one or more tool calls, execute those tools, append the results back into the conversation, and repeat until the model returns a final text response with no tool calls. This pattern is consistent at a high level across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers, though provider message schemas differ. This article uses a normalized abstraction; consult each provider's API reference for exact formats.

Nothing bounds the loop by default. The model alone decides when to stop. If a tool consistently returns an error, the model may retry it. If an external API is flaky, the model has no way to distinguish between transient and permanent failure. The loop simply continues.

Retry storms happen when a tool consistently errors and the model keeps retrying the same call with identical or slightly varied arguments. Then there are semantic loops, where the model cycles between two or more tools without converging on an answer, each tool's output triggering a call to the other. The third failure mode is token blowout: each iteration appends tool call results and model responses to the conversation context, inflating the prompt size and cost linearly, even if the loop eventually terminates.

Note: If you are building with Vite, esbuild, or a similar bundler, you can use "moduleResolution": "bundler" instead. For plain tsc compilation, use "node16" as shown above.

The LLM client is represented as the generic LLMClient interface defined in types.ts. Readers can swap in OpenAI's openai package, Anthropic's @anthropic-ai/sdk, or any compatible client. The guardrails operate on the response shape, not the provider.

This is the structure most tutorials present. It works until it does not.

Each tool is defined with a name, description, a Zod schema for its parameters, and an execute function. Argument validation happens inside the execute wrapper via safeParse, catching hallucinated arguments before they reach application logic.

The createDraftPR tool ties directly back to the Reddit scenario. This pattern mirrors one common resolution for such scenarios: stop and open a draft PR instead of letting the agent loop endlessly. This tutorial encodes that pattern as a generic fallback mechanism.

A per-tool attempt cap tracks how many times a specific tool has been invoked within a single agent run. This is distinct from an overall loop iteration cap. An agent that calls three different tools once each has iterated three times but has zero retries. Meanwhile, an agent that calls the same tool five times in a row because it keeps failing has five attempts on one tool. The per-tool cap catches that. It breaks retry storms while still allowing the agent to use other tools freely.

The guard tracks attempts in a Map<string, number>, scoped to a single run.

When the error fires inside the agent loop, the loop catches it and injects a message telling the model that the tool is unavailable for the remainder of this run. This prevents the model from continuing to request a tool that has already proven it cannot succeed, breaking the retry storm cycle without terminating the entire run.

Long-running agent loops can hang on external API calls that never resolve. An AbortController paired with setTimeout creates a run-level deadline, and Promise.race makes sure the deadline wins even when the work never settles. The AbortSignal is passed to the LLM client so a well-behaved client can cancel its in-flight request.

Important: The AbortSignal only terminates the loop between iterations unless your LLMClient implementation passes it to the underlying HTTP client (e.g., OpenAI SDK's signal option). Verify your client propagates the signal to actually cancel in-flight HTTP requests.

The timeout produces a structured AgentTimeoutResult rather than throwing for abort-caused timeouts. Non-abort errors are still thrown and must be caught by the caller. The caller inspects the result's kind field to determine whether a timeout occurred.

Exact token cost cannot be known before a completion returns. The strategy works on a trailing basis: after each completion, the guard accumulates usage.prompt_tokens and usage.completion_tokens from the response, multiplies by per-token price constants, and compares the running total against a per-run dollar cap. Because it evaluates after each call, it stops the next iteration, not the current one. This is why the guard is labeled "best-effort." A single expensive completion can overshoot the budget before the guard fires.

For hard budget enforcement, set budgetUsd well below your actual limit (e.g., 20% of your ceiling) to absorb worst-case single-call overshoot. The guard cannot prevent a single call from exceeding the budget.

A simple Record<string, { input: number; output: number }> maps model identifiers to per-token costs in dollars. Readers must keep this in sync with their provider's pricing page, as prices change.

Integrating this into the agent loop takes two calls: budget.record(response.usage, model) after each LLM call, and budget.hasExceeded() before the next iteration. When the budget trips, the loop exits into the draft fallback rather than continuing.

When any guardrail trips, the agent should not simply throw an unhandled error or return an empty string. Both outcomes lose the partial work the agent completed before the guardrail fired. The draft-state pattern captures everything collected so far and flags the result as incomplete. Concretely, it preserves all tool outputs accumulated during the run and the full conversation history, so the calling application can inspect what happened, surface it to a human, or retry with adjusted parameters.

cim: AI-ágensek elszabadulása ellen: automatális védőkorlátok TypeScriptben
lead: Egy lépésről lépésre haladó útmutató mutatja be, hogyan előzhetők meg a többezres dolláros számlákat okozó végtelen ciklusok az AI-ágenseknél.
osszefoglalo:
Egy r/cursor Reddit-bejegyzésben számolt be egy fejlesztő arról, hogy az AI-ágense **több mint 2000 dolláros költséget** generált mindössze két óra alatt, mert beragadt egy hibás eszközhívási ciklusba. Mivel a legtöbb LLM SDK nem tartalmaz beépített megszakítót az ágensszintű ciklusokra, a modell automatikusan újrapróbálkozik a hibát dobó eszközökkel, ami végtelen tokenfogyasztáshoz vezet.

A probléma kezelésére a SitePoint egy szolgáltatófüggetlen **TypeScript-alapú védelmi rendszert** mutat be, amely négy különálló korlátot alkalmaz. A rendszer eszközönkénti próbálkozási korlátot, futási időkorlátot (timeout), folyamatosan számolt dolláralapú tokenköltség-keretet, valamint egy alkalmazásszintű tervezetállapot-mentést (DraftResult) használ a részleges eredmények megőrzésére.

A megvalósítás Zod-alapú sémaellenőrzést használ a hallucinált argumentumok kiszűrésére, és tetszőleges LLM-klienssel (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) kombinálható. A megközelítés lényege, hogy hiba esetén az ágens nem egyszerűen leáll, hanem elmenti az eddigi beszélgetési előzményeket és eszközválaszokat a későbbi emberi ellenőrzéshez.
miert_szamit: Az AI-ágenseket fejlesztők és üzemeltetők **megelőzhetik a váratlan és extrém magas API-számlákat**, miközben stabilabbá és biztonságosabbá tehetik az automatizált munkafolyamatokat.
